STABL Stability Selection (Beginner Interface)

Source: R/stabl.R
stabl.Rd

One-stop-shop stability selection for biomarker discovery. Give it a table of features and an outcome; it runs STABL with statistically safe defaults and returns an object that tells you, in plain language, which features were selected and how reliable the selection is.

Usage

stabl(
  x,
  y,
  family = "gaussian",
  base_learner = "lasso",
  n_bootstraps = 1000L,
  random_state = NULL,
  ...
)

Arguments

x

A data.frame or numeric matrix of predictors (samples \(\times\) features). A data.frame may contain the outcome as a column (see y). Row names become sample IDs when present; otherwise IDs are generated as s1, s2, ....

y

The outcome. One of: a vector (numeric, character, or factor) aligned to x's rows (by names when both are named, otherwise by position); or, when x is a data.frame, a length-1 character naming the outcome column, which is then removed from the predictors.

family

Character; "gaussian" (default), "binomial", "multinomial", or "cox". Use "binomial" for two-class outcomes, "multinomial" for more.

base_learner

Character; "lasso" (default), "elastic_net", "adaptive_lasso", "sparse_group_lasso", or "rf".

n_bootstraps

Integer; bootstrap iterations per lambda. Default 1000L (the published STABL default); lower it only for quick exploration.

random_state

Integer or NULL; seed for reproducibility.

...

Additional arguments forwarded to stabl_fit() (the expert interface), e.g. artificial_proportion, sample_fraction, sample_groups, knockoff_fallback.

Value

An object of class c("stabl", "stabl_fit"). Print it for a plain-language answer; use summary(), plot(), get_support(), get_feature_names(), and get_fdrs() for details. All stabl_fit accessors and workflows apply unchanged.

Details

This is the recommended entry point for new users. It wraps the expert interface stabl_fit() with opinionated defaults:

  • artificial_type = "knockoff_equi" — model-X knockoff artificial features, the pairing validated for FDP+ calibration (the package default "random_permutation" is retained on the expert interface for Python-parity workflows but is anti-conservative for multivariate learners).

  • FDP+ calibration on (no hard_threshold), strict knockoff fallback (knockoff_fallback = "stop").

  • Automatic lambda grid (always: stabl() fixes lambda_grid to "auto"; supply a manual grid via stabl_fit() if needed).

Everything else — other learners, bootstrap design, thresholds, groups — is one ... away: unnamed arguments in ... are forwarded to stabl_fit(), which documents the full expert interface.

See also

stabl_fit() for the expert interface; get_feature_names() for the selected features; compute_fdp_plus() for the calibration machinery.

Examples

set.seed(1L)
df <- data.frame(
  age  = rnorm(40),
  m1   = rnorm(40), m2 = rnorm(40), m3 = rnorm(40),
  m4   = rnorm(40), m5 = rnorm(40)
)
df$y <- 0.8 * df$m1 + 0.8 * df$m2 + rnorm(40, sd = 0.5)
# \donttest{
fit <- stabl(df, y = "y", n_bootstraps = 50L, random_state = 1L)
fit                      # plain-language print
#> <stabl stability selection>
#>   outcome family: gaussian | base learner: lasso | bootstraps: 50
#>   5 feature(s) selected at FDP+ estimate 1.000:
#>   m1, m2, m3, m4, m5
#>   use summary() for details, plot() for stability paths,
#>   get_feature_names() / get_support() for the selection,
#>   get_fdrs() for the FDP+ curve.
get_feature_names(fit)   # selected features
#> [1] "m1" "m2" "m3" "m4" "m5"
# }
